author: m0_ox
content:
> OTOH if I have to do the work of parsing all the AI slop that is sent my way I'd be burned out in less than a week.

This is true for sure. But is it unreasonable to think that a Mythos harness can run and vet / read the code + reproduce _all_ of these and rank them even based on "not enough evidence but potentially high risk" and things like these? I think the majority of the work these days can be put into good prompts and harness building at least as a first step of filtering (slice of cheese in swiss cheese model). It wouldn't stop at 1 wrong statement as humans can do... it could actually try to get to the claim, try to repro, read the code, and try to rank, etc... give a confidence score.

I think every client team should have at least some version of this running on a server somewhere trying to reproduce and grade these findings. There's a weakness here as well that humans may rely on this list and what if it ranks something lower that should be higher, etc... but perhaps the human verification happens side by side to this harness and this is just one more Swiss cheese slice in the workflow whereas in today's world it just gets "closed".

If these models are out here solving the Riemann Hypothesis, under a good harness and prompting we _can_ get to all CVEs in a more structured way I think. Maybe that's a naive thought.

I hope you are not implying that my work is AI slop. What I have reported lines up exactly with the second part of your story. This is a vulnerability that was ignored but is ultimately impactful to Lighthouse.

I won't speak on this further at <@602753420033785856>  request, but I will say that Ethereum is absolutely massive, so any security-related issues brought to your teams should be taken seriously, and your teams should be less dismissive.

As <@796570016966770688> pointed out, AI is able to solve math problems that have stumped humans for over a century, and for a while now, it has been able to find critical-severity vulnerabilities in many platforms. Just recently, OpenAI found over 1,000 vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel.
